title: Reliable long-horizon mortality and longevity forecasting with honest uncertainty

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a broadly transferable framework for forecasting how mortality at different ages—and therefore population longevity—may change over decades. It would combine demographic patterns with relevant causal evidence, provide uncertainty ranges that hold up under evaluation, and warn when changing conditions make historical relationships unreliable. Its value would include knowing when a precise forecast is no longer justified.

The motivation is that extrapolative methods such as Lee–Carter assume that past mortality trends will continue. The supplied validation study finds that this approach can work well in some populations and mortality regimes but perform poorly when developments become discontinuous. The study also recognizes explanatory approaches incorporating health behavior and risk factors, so incorporating information beyond historical mortality trends is already an existing research direction. The proposed advance is dependable integration and demonstrated transfer across settings, rather than simply adding explanatory variables to a model.

As a proposed scope, the framework would account for medical developments, epidemics, behavior and social conditions where evidence allows, while explicitly representing uncertainty about changes it cannot anticipate. It would forecast population outcomes rather than individual lifespans. The supplied evidence motivates this target but does not establish either its achievement or its complete absence across the field.

significance.text: Mortality forecasts inform planning for pensions and other social security systems. The supplied study emphasizes that decision makers need to understand where forecasting methods are suitable, making reliability across different mortality regimes consequential for long-term commitments.

As a conditional actuarial implication, a substantial and durable improvement could improve reserve setting, lifetime-annuity valuation and assessment of retirement promises. This benefit depends on forecasts transferring from the general populations used in validation to the particular pension and insured populations whose liabilities are being valued. Better estimates could reduce avoidable funding errors, but no financial reduction is quantified by the supplied evidence.

A particularly valuable capability would distinguish situations where a forecast remains informative from those where structural change makes uncertainty too large for a precise estimate. Such warnings could support contingency planning and more explicit treatment of uncertain future obligations. Revolutionary significance would depend on the scale, breadth and persistence of the improvement; a better validation workflow for an existing model would not by itself establish this breakthrough.

These benefits have practical limits. Accurate mortality forecasts would not guarantee pension sustainability, remove investment risk or determine suitable contribution levels and retirement-income designs on their own. Nor would the framework need to predict every future medical discovery or pandemic precisely. Its contribution would be better mortality-sensitive decisions under uncertainty.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is reliable integration of demographic and causal evidence with calibrated uncertainty and useful warnings about structural change. The supplied study establishes a narrower problem: Lee–Carter performance varies with population, mortality regime and outcome measure. Because it evaluates one extrapolative method and discusses alternative approaches without comprehensively assessing them, it cannot establish a field-wide absence of the proposed combined capability.

As a scientific synthesis, a central barrier is distinguishing relationships that will persist from patterns specific to a historical setting. A causal relationship useful for forecasting also requires information about how its drivers may evolve. Medical progress, health behavior and social conditions can themselves be uncertain, and their effects may differ across populations. Incorporating such evidence therefore needs an evaluation design suited to explanatory forecasting; the supplied review notes that the paper limits the applicability of its particular workflow to explanatory approaches.

As methodological requirements of the proposal, uncertainty estimates must capture more than ordinary variation around an extrapolated trend. They must be evaluated for whether they remain informative when assumptions weaken, without relying on intervals so broad that they offer little decision value. Structural-change warnings also face a tradeoff: warnings that arrive too late provide little protection, while frequent false alarms can undermine their usefulness.

Long horizons create an additional validation barrier. Direct prospective evaluation takes decades, and historical forecasts with overlapping outcome periods do not provide fully independent evidence. Retrospective tests must also reconstruct what information was actually available at each forecast origin. Population transfer adds another challenge: success for national mortality does not automatically establish usefulness for a particular pension scheme or insured group.

current_state.text: Ricarda Duerst, Jonas Schöley and Christina Bohk-Ewald’s April 2023 MPIDR Working Paper 2023-020, A Validation Workflow for Mortality Forecasting, evaluates Lee–Carter using rolling out-of-sample validation. Its application uses 30-year base periods to produce 20-year mortality forecasts. The principal performance measures are point-forecast errors in life expectancy and lifespan disparity at birth, providing distinct assessments of average longevity and the spread of ages at death.

The authors report suitable performance in many high-income, low-mortality settings with smooth developments, particularly in the later historical observations included in their study. They also report poorer performance in some historical regimes with discontinuous developments. Suitability consequently depends on population, regime and mortality measure. These are the authors’ reported findings from a dated historical evaluation; the reference to later observations does not establish performance in 2026.

This work demonstrates an evaluation workflow and reports evidence about an existing forecasting model. It does not demonstrate the proposed long-horizon causal framework, calibrated uncertainty intervals or effective structural-change warnings. Although the paper discusses uncertainty and cites interval-forecasting research, its inspected analysis evaluates point estimates. Those references alone do not establish how uncertainty estimates are constructed or how well they are calibrated. This limitation does not show that uncertainty forecasting is unavailable elsewhere.

The paper’s front matter states that MPIDR working papers receive only limited review. According to the supplied review and source index, its identity was verified and the retained text covered all 28 pages without truncation or reported extraction issues. The review did not independently verify the plotted results. Thus the supplied record supports attribution of the findings to the authors, with the paper’s review status and the limits of the evidence review preserved.

The supplied material does not establish the field’s status as of November 1, 2026. Its freshness record contains no assessment of subsequent developments, and the later retrieval date of the saved PDF does not update the study’s findings. Whether newer work achieves substantial parts of the proposed capability remains an open question in this record.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: register age-specific mortality forecasts and uncertainty ranges before outcomes are known, across multiple populations and horizons. Combine historical holdouts spanning different mortality regimes with accumulating prospective observations. Historical tests should use only information available at each forecast origin, including contemporaneously available explanatory variables and assumptions. The supplied study grounds the use of rolling historical validation; preregistration and the additional requirements here are proposed extensions.
completion_criteria.label: Validate preregistered mortality forecasts and uncertainty across populations and horizons

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evaluation: specify established comparators, calibration measures, decision-relevant losses and thresholds for material improvement in advance. Assess age-specific mortality as well as derived outcomes such as life expectancy and lifespan disparity, since success on one summary measure need not establish success on another. Evaluate uncertainty-range coverage together with informativeness, and report performance by population and mortality regime so that aggregate gains do not conceal important failures. These choices would be demonstration criteria, not established standards supplied by the source.
completion_criteria.label: Report prespecified comparative forecast evaluation across populations and mortality regimes

completion_criteria.text: Proposed warning test: assess whether warnings about structural shifts are timely and informative, including false alarms, missed changes and the consequences of acting on them. A convincing framework should indicate when its estimates become less reliable and show whether its stated uncertainty remains appropriate during those periods. It need not identify the exact timing or nature of every future invention, epidemic or social change.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrate timely, informative structural-shift warnings and appropriate uncertainty

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and transfer test: make model specifications, evaluation procedures, forecast-origin information and results available for independent reproduction, subject to legitimate data-access restrictions. Where those restrictions prevent full reproduction, state what independent checks remain possible. Test transfer separately to relevant pension and insured populations before claiming corresponding valuation benefits, and distinguish observed improvements from projected financial consequences.
completion_criteria.label: Enable independent reproduction and test pension and insured-population transfer

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evidential boundary: claims about 50-year performance would require long-run historical evaluation that accounts for dependence among overlapping forecast periods, alongside accumulating prospective evidence. Short prospective tests alone could not validate such claims. Even a successful program would establish demonstrated breadth across the tested populations, horizons and regimes; finite tests could not establish literal universality or reliability under every future structural change.
completion_criteria.label: Bound 50-year performance claims using dependence-aware long-run evaluation

related_concepts.text: Based on the supplied roster titles, ACT-01, Reliable actuarial measurement of unprecedented catastrophe losses, shares the challenge of reasoning about conditions poorly represented in historical data. ACT-04 concerns age-specific mortality trajectories and longevity over time; ACT-01 concerns catastrophe losses. Their uncertainty problems overlap without making their forecasting targets interchangeable.

Based on the supplied roster title, ACT-02, Trustworthy, near-instant insurance settlement at negligible per-claim cost, addresses the speed, cost and trustworthiness of settling claims. ACT-04 addresses forecasting mortality before future outcomes occur. Improvements in either could support insurance operations, but settlement performance would not demonstrate mortality-forecast reliability.

Based on the supplied roster title, ACT-03, A scalable actuarial architecture for financing correlated catastrophes, concerns financing correlated losses. ACT-04 concerns measuring future mortality and its uncertainty. Epidemics could connect the two topics, but a forecasting capability and a financing architecture solve different parts of a risk-management problem.

Based on the supplied roster title, ACT-05, Dependable long-horizon economic scenarios for actuarial liabilities, is closely related through long horizons, structural change and liability assessment. Its forecast targets are economic conditions, whereas ACT-04 targets mortality. Joint applications could require coherent treatment of both, but accurate economic scenarios would not establish accurate longevity forecasts, or vice versa.

Based on the supplied roster title, ACT-06, Reliable long-term actuarial projection of healthcare costs under structural change, overlaps through changing health conditions and medical developments. Its outcome is healthcare cost, which also depends on factors beyond mortality. Longer lives do not by themselves determine future healthcare spending, so the two projection tasks remain distinct.

The supplied title of ACT-07, Accessible lifetime retirement income through transparent, resilient risk pooling, supports a limited distinction between retirement-income design and ACT-04’s mortality forecasting. Better longevity estimates could inform the pricing and evaluation of lifetime-income pools, while pool design determines how risks and resources are shared. The roster does not supply ACT-07’s detailed mechanism or requirements, so this relationship is a title-based interpretation.

change_log.change: Preserved ACT-04’s identity and integrated the framework’s demographic, causal, uncertainty and structural-change components into a single explanation.
change_log.reason: The concept remains coherent even though the supplied evidence does not establish its field-wide availability or absence.

change_log.change: Replaced broad claims about standard projections with a specific account of extrapolative Lee–Carter assumptions and acknowledged existing explanatory approaches.
change_log.reason: The retained study supports these distinctions but does not characterize every mortality-forecasting method.

change_log.change: Specified the April 2023 study’s 30-year base periods, 20-year forecasts and principal point-error measures.
change_log.reason: These details define the demonstrated scope and prevent an inference that the study validates 50-year forecasts or uncertainty calibration.

change_log.change: Qualified the earlier assertion about existing uncertainty estimates and separated uncertainty discussion from demonstrated calibration.
change_log.reason: The inspected analysis evaluates point forecasts; discussion and bibliography entries do not establish uncertainty construction or performance.

change_log.change: Preserved regime-dependent findings, limited-review status and the supplied review’s extraction and verification boundaries.
change_log.reason: The findings remain useful with appropriate attribution; complete text extraction does not independently verify plotted results.

change_log.change: Made pension and insured-population transfer explicit and distinguished conditional financial benefits from measured outcomes.
change_log.reason: General-population forecasting success does not automatically establish valuation gains for particular liability populations.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed demonstrations to address information leakage, overlapping holdouts, predefined performance criteria, warning usefulness and reproducibility.
change_log.reason: These refinements make the proposed capability assessable while preserving their status as proposals rather than achieved results or established standards.

change_log.change: Explained relationships with every other supplied roster entry and retained a qualified ACT-07 comparison.
change_log.reason: The roster supports title-based distinctions, including retirement-income risk pooling, while providing no detailed specifications for neighboring concepts.

change_log.change: Separated the dated study’s findings from unresolved field-wide status in 2026.
change_log.reason: An empty freshness assessment and a later retrieval date cannot establish subsequent scientific progress.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not determine whether work available by November 1, 2026 achieves the full framework or substantial components of it.
Evidence for construction and calibration of mortality uncertainty estimates beyond the inspected point-forecast study is not supplied; this is an evidence gap, not evidence of nonexistence.
Material-improvement thresholds, comparators, calibration measures, financial loss functions and acceptable warning performance remain to be specified for a concrete demonstration.
Transfer to pension and insured populations, and resulting reductions in funding or valuation errors, remain un demonstrated in the supplied record.

The review recommended removing or independently checking ACT-07’s scope attribution. The final record retains only a title-based comparison because the supplied roster explicitly identifies lifetime retirement income and risk pooling; its detailed scope remains unknown.
The supplied review reports complete extraction but does not independently verify plotted results. No independent replication or later review outcome is supplied.

brief.title: Reliable forecasts of how long populations will live
possible: People planning pensions could anticipate how long populations may live decades ahead, with uncertainty ranges they can trust. They could also get warnings when changing conditions make precise forecasts unreliable.
Forecasts would combine past patterns of deaths at different ages with evidence about medicine, epidemics, behavior and social conditions. They would describe whole populations.
why: Pension planners and insurers could better estimate the money needed to meet future promises. Better forecasts could reduce avoidable errors in funding and in valuing payments that continue throughout retirement.
Warnings that a forecast has become unreliable could help planners prepare alternatives and account more explicitly for uncertain future obligations.

sources.who: Ricarda Duerst, Jonas Schöley and Christina Bohk-Ewald
sources.showed: Their working paper, which received limited review, tested Lee–Carter, a model that extends past death-rate trends. It performed well in many countries with smooth trends but poorly during some abrupt changes.
sources.quote:
We show that the mortality regime in the country of interest plays a crucial role
for the performance of a forecast method.
sources.cited_for: Forecast reliability depends on the population and on how death rates change over time.
sources.not_established: The study does not demonstrate reliable uncertainty ranges, warnings of changing conditions or integration of causal evidence.

sources.showed: Their neural networks, computer models that learn patterns, reduced forecast errors across many countries. They also produced uncertainty ranges that reliably contained observed death rates in their tests.
sources.quote: find that lower forecast errors are achievable for many countries in the Human Mortality Database.
sources.cited_for: Learning from mortality patterns can improve forecasts and produce useful uncertainty ranges.
sources.not_established: These tests do not establish reliable forecasts across future abrupt changes or integration of causal evidence.

shown: Duerst and colleagues tested forecasts against later historical outcomes, showing where extending past trends succeeds or fails. Schnürch and Korn went further on uncertainty, reporting useful forecast ranges alongside improved predictions across countries.
Some of Schnürch and Korn’s longer tests used model settings chosen with information from the test period. That limits how closely those results represent forecasting an unknown future.
missing: A combined framework still needs to demonstrate that evidence about causes improves forecasts across populations and changing conditions.
Uncertainty ranges need to stay dependable and useful when historical patterns break down.
Warnings need to arrive early enough to help, without too many false alarms.
Long-term reliability and transfer to pension members and insured groups need separate demonstrations.

milestones.label: Forecasts registered before outcomes hold up across populations
milestones.explanation: Forecasts for deaths at different ages and their uncertainty ranges would have to pass historical and future tests using only information available beforehand. This would test reliability across populations and forecast lengths.

milestones.label: Comparisons show useful gains across different mortality patterns
milestones.explanation: Tests agreed in advance would have to show gains over established methods across death rates, average lifespan, its spread and uncertainty ranges. This would keep overall gains from hiding important failures.

milestones.label: Timely warnings identify when forecasts become unreliable
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to show useful warnings of changing death-rate patterns, accounting for false alarms, missed changes and appropriate uncertainty. This would establish when planners should place less trust in a forecast.

milestones.label: Independent reproduction and transfer to pension and insured populations
milestones.explanation: Independent researchers would have to reproduce results where data access allows, and tests would have to establish transfer to pension members and insured groups. This would support claims about retirement and insurance planning.

milestones.label: Long-run tests support bounded claims about 50-year forecasts
milestones.explanation: Long historical tests would have to account for shared outcomes in overlapping forecasts, alongside accumulating future observations. This would support long-range claims within tested settings without implying universal reliability.

uncertain: Which medical, behavioral and social relationships will persist, and how well can their future drivers be forecast?
What improvement, uncertainty-range accuracy and warning performance would count as useful enough for decisions?
How far can success in tested populations and historical conditions support confidence under future changes?

page.title: Probabilistic mortality forecasting under structural change
page.definition: Population forecasts of age-specific death rates and life expectancy extend 20 years ahead using mortality histories and risk-factor evidence. Their probability intervals cover outcomes at least as often as stated, and responses to detected changes in mortality trends improve forecast scores.

goal.need: Pension valuation depends on how long payments continue. The IMF quantified this exposure with a three-year longevity shock in a pension model; the table gives liability increases at two discount rates. The model assumed entry at age 20, retirement at 60, and inflation-indexed benefits linked to final salary.

figures.caption: IMF pension-model sensitivity to increased longevity, April 2012
figures.note: Conditional model calculations, expressed relative to liabilities before the longevity shock.

completion.title: Independent validation confirms 20-year mortality forecast gains through changes in mortality trends.
completion.criterion: Independent investigators evaluate a fixed risk-factor mortality framework on withheld 20-year periods spanning mortality-trend changes, in populations excluded from development. Using only forecast-origin information, it beats Lee–Carter on life-expectancy mean absolute error and mean 95% interval score; its nominal 95% intervals attain at least 95% coverage. Enabling its structural-change warning response lowers mean interval score versus disabling it. The findings are independently reproduced and accepted after peer review; uncertainty in comparisons accounts for overlapping forecast periods.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no outside body located defines an acceptance test for this combined capability.
completion.basis: Searches of OECD mortality-table guidance, SOA research calls and mortality-validation studies found no acceptance test for the combined capability. This Atlas fallback joins published 20-year backtesting, benchmark comparison and interval evaluation to SOA's turning-point objective. Neither the combined test nor the choice of 20 years is a professional certification standard.

milestones.title: A risk-factor model forecasts life expectancy with lower mean absolute error than Lee–Carter.
milestones.criterion: Life-expectancy forecasts have lower mean absolute error than Lee–Carter on the same countries, sexes and withheld periods. Li and Raftery's smoking-adjusted model met this comparison in 67 countries for 2000–2015: errors were 0.962 versus 2.043 years for males and 0.728 versus 1.210 years for females. Training covered 1950–2000; observations were organised in five-year periods.
milestones.set_by: Mortality-forecast evaluation convention: lower out-of-sample error than an established benchmark, applied by Li and Raftery (2021), section 4, and Schnürch and Korn (2022), section 4.2. These comparisons specify no universal minimum effect size.
milestones.threshold_quote: Our method had the smallest MAE for both sexes and both choices of test period among the five methods.

milestones.title: Nominal 95% mortality prediction intervals attain at least 95% empirical coverage.
milestones.criterion: Observed death rates fall inside nominal 95% prediction intervals at least 95% of the time; interval width is assessed separately. Schnürch and Korn evaluated 54 sex-specific national populations, ages 60–89, over 2007–2016, training through 2006. Feedforward and convolutional neural networks achieved pooled coverage of 97.0% and 98.0%, respectively. Pooled coverage does not establish coverage within every population or horizon.
milestones.set_by: Nominal-coverage evaluation convention, applied at 95% by Schnürch and Korn (2022), section 4.3. The at-least-95% cutoff is their study-specific implementation; coverage and width are also evaluated by Li and Raftery (2021).
milestones.threshold_quote: Good prediction intervals should minimize MPIW under the constraint that PICP is at or above the specified threshold a.

milestones.title: One mortality model combines 20-year forecast gains, 95% coverage and improved scores after warnings.
milestones.criterion: A developer demonstrates one risk-factor mortality model on withheld 20-year periods spanning changes in mortality trends. Using only forecast-origin information, it beats Lee–Carter on life-expectancy mean absolute error and mean 95% interval score, attains at least 95% coverage for nominal 95% intervals, and lowers mean interval score when its warning response is enabled rather than disabled. The interval score penalizes width and missed observations. Fu et al. reported retrospective structural-change analysis in six countries and 5- and 10-year forecast comparisons; those results do not establish this combined test.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback: searches of OECD guidance, SOA research calls and mortality-validation papers found no external criterion for a combined developer demonstration. The 20-year horizon follows Duerst et al.'s published example, not a field-wide requirement.

not_found: No regulator, actuarial standard, government programme or prize acceptance test was found for the combined capability.
No published independent validation was located that satisfies the combined completion test.
No external numerical acceptance thresholds were found for warning lead time, false alarms or transfer to pension and insured populations.
No published validation was located establishing the combined capability over a 50-year horizon.
